slides.title: Booleans and truthiness
slides.sub: The two-valued algebra under every decision
slides.notes:
SAY: Chapter 1 introduced the value as a piece of data that a program can compute with, and it named three kinds of value: integers, floating-point numbers and strings. Chapter 2 adds a fourth kind, the Boolean value, which has only two members, True and False, and which answers a yes-or-no question (Sweigart, 2025).

slides.title: The man inside the bool type

items.cap: George Boole - public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

items: A shoemaker's son from Lincoln, self-taught
1847 and 1854: reasoning itself obeys algebra
He never saw a computer; every circuit runs his logic
Python's True-and-False type carries his name: bool

items.who: George Boole, self-taught mathematician, first professor of mathematics at Cork
items.where: Lincoln, England and Queen's College, Cork

slides.notes:
STORY (1847 and 1854): A shoemaker's son from Lincoln taught himself mathematics, and in 'The Mathematical Analysis of Logic' (1847) and 'The Laws of Thought' (1854) showed that reasoning itself obeys algebra: statements as values, AND and OR as operations. He never saw a computer. A century later his algebra became the switching logic of every circuit, and Python names its True-and-False type bool after him - every condition on today's slides is Boole's arithmetic.
SOURCE: George Boole, 'The Mathematical Analysis of Logic' (1847) and 'An Investigation of the Laws of Thought' (1854); biography at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Boole. Portrait: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
slides.take: Every if statement runs on one Victorian's algebra

items: Same five lines, one space of difference - and two different programs
A lesson carried from the ABC language: what you see is what the interpreter sees

items.cap: program indent_in_v1_0_0.py, lines 1 to 5 of 5, run under Python 3.13.16
items.label: 'always' inside the block

items.cap: program indent_out_v1_0_0.py, lines 1 to 5 of 5, run under Python 3.13.16
items.label: 'always' outside - it prints

items.who: Guido van Rossum, carrying a lesson from the ABC language at CWI
items.where: documented in Python's own design FAQ

slides.notes:
STORY (design decision of the late 1980s): Most languages mark blocks with braces and treat indentation as decoration; Python makes the indentation itself the block. The choice came from ABC, the teaching language Guido van Rossum worked on at CWI before Python, and the design FAQ still defends it: what you see is what the interpreter sees, so a program cannot look right and group wrong. The chapter's two indentation programs run the same lines indented two ways - and print different stories.
SOURCE: The Python design FAQ, 'Why does Python use indentation for grouping of statements?' (docs.python.org/3/faq/design.html); the ABC lineage per van Rossum's documented history of the language.
slides.take: In Python the layout cannot lie about the logic

slides.notes:
STORY (accepted 2021-02; shipped 2021-10 in Python 3.10): For decades Python answered 'where is my switch statement?' with dictionaries and elif chains. In February 2021 the Steering Council accepted structural pattern matching - PEPs 634, 635 and 636 - and Python 3.10 shipped the match statement that October. It is more than a switch: patterns destructure data and bind names. The chapter's match programs - command words, status codes, captures, guards - run the real thing, and their transcripts are on these slides.
SOURCE: PEP 634/635/636 (structural pattern matching), accepted by the Python Steering Council in February 2021; first released in Python 3.10, October 2021. Tutorial: peps.python.org/pep-0636.
slides.take: match is a 2021 feature - you saw it arrive
